title: Producers II: batching, acks and idempotence
goal: By the end, you can explain what happens between `send()` and the broker's answer, tune how long records wait to travel together, read a timeout correctly as "unknown", and say what Kafka's idempotent producer prevents and what it doesn't.
opening:
You send a message to a friend from a train as it goes into a tunnel. A little clock appears beside it, then the message turns red: not sent. You tap Retry. Out of the tunnel, your friend writes back: "Why did you send that twice?"

The red mark looked like a fact about the message. It was only a fact about your phone: it had stopped waiting. The first copy had got through. That's an easy trap, because an error usually means nothing happened.

Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages and lets other programs read them, sets the same trap for the programs that write to it. Producers I: keys, partitions and ordering decided which partition gets each payment. In this lesson, we'll follow a payment from `send()` to the broker's answer. We'll watch records wait in batches, freeze a broker until sends fail, and find the failed payments in the log anyway. Then we'll meet the setting that stops retries from writing a payment twice. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The payments app sends a payment to Kafka with default settings. Two minutes later the send fails with an error called `TimeoutException`. What do you know about the payment?
options: It wasn't written: the producer gave up before the broker stored it
It may or may not be in the log
It's in the log exactly once, because a duplicate check is on by default
It's in the log, but marked as failed, so readers skip it
warmup.why: The timeout means the producer stopped waiting, not that the broker never wrote the record. The broker can store a payment while its answer gets lost on the way back, or a frozen broker can store it after the producer has given up. The Try it in the third section finds four such payments in the log. The duplicate check, the idempotent producer of the last section, stops the producer's own retries from writing a payment twice, but it can't tell you whether this one made it. And Kafka has no "failed" mark on records.

sections.h: send() puts the payment in a batch and returns at once
sections.body:
Picture the busiest minute of the day. The payments app sends 20,000 records a second to Kafka, one for each payment or refund. What if every `send()` became its own message over the network, and waited for its answer? Two things would go wrong.

A round trip, a message to a broker and its answer back, takes about half a millisecond inside one data centre, a building full of computers. Code that waits for each answer in turn manages about 2,000 sends a second, a tenth of what we need. And the broker would handle 20,000 requests a second, each with its own headers, checks and write to disk, for records of a few hundred bytes. Most of its work would be paperwork.

The producer, the part of the Kafka library that sends records, avoids both with one design: `send()` doesn't send anything. (Every default in this lesson is the Kafka 4.4 producer's.) It does three things in your code's thread and returns. A thread is one line of work inside a program, and a program can run several side by side. The three things:

1. It serializes the key and the value, which means it turns them into bytes.
2. It picks the partition (Producers I: keys, partitions and ordering).
3. It adds the record to a batch for that partition, in a buffer called the **record accumulator**. Then it returns a `Future<RecordMetadata>`, an object that will hold the answer once it arrives.

A batch is a group of records for one partition that travels together. Your phone in the tunnel did something similar: it put the message in a queue, showed the little clock, and sent it when it could.

A separate thread inside the producer, the **sender**, does the network work while your code carries on. It takes the batches that are ready (the next section says when) and groups them by the broker that leads their partition. Then it sends one request per broker, carrying batches for many partitions at once. When an answer comes back, it fills in each record's `Future` and runs its callback, a function you hand to `send()` for the producer to call later.

So the return of `send()` means "queued", not "written". You learn the outcome from the `Future` or from the callback:

```java
producer.send(record, (metadata, e) -> {
    if (e != null) log.warn("payment {} not confirmed", id, e);   // runs on the sender thread
});
```

```kotlin
producer.send(record) { metadata, e ->
    if (e != null) log.warn("payment {} not confirmed", id, e)     // runs on the sender thread
}
```

Calling `send(record).get()` on every record throws the design away. `get()` waits for the answer, so your thread waits out every round trip, and every batch carries one record. Use the callback, or keep the futures and check them later. `flush()` waits until everything queued so far has an answer, and `close()` does the same before it shuts the producer down.

`send()` can still make you wait, in two cases. The first send to a topic waits for the topic's metadata: how many partitions it has, and which brokers lead them. And when the accumulator's memory, `buffer.memory` (32 MiB by default), is full because the brokers are slower than your code, `send()` waits for space. Both waits end after `max.block.ms`, one minute by default, with an exception.

One more thing follows from the design. The producer is thread-safe: many threads may call `send()` on one producer at the same time. The `KafkaProducer` documentation says that one producer shared by all threads is generally faster than several, because their records share batches.

So the records now wait in batches. Next, we'll see what decides when a batch leaves.

sections.h: A batch leaves when it's full or when linger.ms runs out
sections.body:
The sender needs a rule for when a batch may leave. Sent too early, it carries one record. Held too long, every payment waits. Kafka uses two settings, per partition, and the post room of a busy office makes them easy to picture.

In the post room, each city gets its own mailbag. A bag goes out when it's full, or when the van leaves, every few minutes, whichever comes first. The bag is the batch, the city is the partition, and the van's timetable is the longest a record may wait.

`batch.size` is the most a batch may hold: 16,384 bytes (16 KB) by default. When the next record doesn't fit, the batch is closed, and a closed batch may leave at once.

`linger.ms` is how long a batch may wait for more records: 5 ms by default. A batch that is 5 ms old may leave even if it holds one record. Until Kafka 4.0 the default was 0, which meant "send as soon as the sender is free". The producer documentation explains the change: bigger batches are so much cheaper to handle that the total delay usually ends up about the same or lower, despite the wait.

Let's put numbers on it. At 1,000 records a second for one partition, a record arrives every millisecond. With `linger.ms=5`, each batch collects about 5 records before it leaves. With 50, it collects about 50, and each record waits up to 50 ms longer. A burst behaves differently. When 170 records of 100 bytes arrive at once, 163 of them fill a batch to 16 KB, and that batch leaves straight away, without waiting. The stepper below walks through both cases. Here the post room picture breaks a little: Kafka has no shared timetable. Each bag has its own clock, which starts when its first letter goes in.

`linger.ms=0` doesn't mean one record per request, either. The producer keeps up to 5 requests in flight, sent but not yet answered, on each connection to a broker (`max.in.flight.requests.per.connection`). When all 5 are waiting for answers, new records pile up in the accumulator and leave together in the next request. So under heavy load, batches form anyway. `linger.ms` matters most when traffic is moderate, where the sender would otherwise send small batches as fast as it can.

Batches are also where compression happens: making the bytes smaller by writing repeated patterns only once. With `compression.type` set to `lz4`, `zstd`, `snappy` or `gzip` (four common methods), the producer compresses each batch as one unit. The broker stores the compressed batch as it arrived; the topic's default, `compression.type=producer`, means "keep what the producer sent". The consumer decompresses it. Payment records repeat the same field names and currencies, so they compress well, and bigger batches compress better, because there's more repetition to find.

The Try it measures all of this from the producer's own counters. Next, we'll see what the producer does when the answer to a batch is an error, or doesn't come at all.

try.title: Measure batching from the producer's own metrics
steps: From the `labs` folder, start a one-broker Kafka with `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait` (Docker runs it in a container, a sealed-off box on your computer). Then create a topic with one partition: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic ledger-events --partitions 1`.

Predict the records per request for `linger.ms` 0, 5 and 50, at about 1,000 records a second. Then run the demo (command below). It sends 500 payment records per setting and prints four of the producer's metrics, the counters it keeps about itself: `records-per-request-avg`, `batch-size-avg`, `compression-rate-avg` and `record-queue-time-avg`.
Keep the broker running for the next Try its.

The bytes per batch include a header of about 60 bytes per batch, one more reason one-record batches waste space. Your timings will differ by a few milliseconds; the shape won't.

sections.h: Retries happen on their own, inside one deadline
sections.body:
The broker answers each request once the partition's leader has done what the producer asked. The cluster: KRaft, replicas and the ISR covered that with the `acks` setting. With `acks=all`, the default since Kafka 3.0, the leader waits until every copy that is keeping up, every in-sync replica, has the batch. With `acks=1`, it answers once its own copy has it. With `acks=0`, the producer doesn't wait for any answer, so it never learns an offset (the answer says -1) or an error.

Answers can be errors. Some are retriable: the problem may pass if the producer tries again. `NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER` (the partition's leader moved to another broker), `NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS` (too few copies in sync) and a request that timed out are all retriable. Others aren't. A record bigger than the broker allows, or a missing permission, fails the send at once.

For retriable errors, the producer retries on its own. `retries` defaults to 2,147,483,647, the biggest number an `int` can hold, so in effect forever. Between attempts it pauses, starting at 100 ms and doubling up to 1 second. Each attempt waits at most `request.timeout.ms`, 30 seconds by default, for its answer.

"Forever" has an end, and one setting decides it: **`delivery.timeout.ms`**, 2 minutes by default. Its clock starts when `send()` returns, and it covers everything after that: the time in the batch, the wait for a free request slot, every attempt and every pause. When it runs out, the producer fails the record with a `TimeoutException`. The producer insists that this deadline is at least `linger.ms` plus `request.timeout.ms`. The documentation's advice is to leave `retries` alone and set this deadline instead.

Now the part that matters most for payments, and it's the red mark from the train. A `TimeoutException` tells you the producer gave up waiting. It doesn't tell you the record is missing. Picture a request that reached the broker and was added to the log, but whose answer was lost. Or picture a broker that froze while your request waited in its network buffer, the space where incoming bytes wait to be read. It handled the request after the producer had given up. The Try it below does exactly that. It freezes the broker for 8 seconds while payments flow with a 5-second deadline. Five sends fail, and four of those five are in the log anyway.

**A failed send means unknown. Treat it as unknown.**

Code that treats it as "not written" and sends the payment again as new, or tells the customer it failed, gets it wrong some of the time. That's the friend with two copies of your message. The safe move is to send it again with the same idempotency key, a unique id made once per payment and sent with every attempt. The consumer then drops the copy it has already seen. Calling other services: REST, RPC and gRPC built that idea, and Consumers: the poll loop, offsets and delivery guarantees builds the consumer that checks it.

The producer's own retries cause trouble of their own, though, even when no deadline passes. Next, we'll see how, and Kafka's fix.

aside.title: Why not set the deadline to an hour, so sends never fail?
aside.body: Because something is usually waiting on the answer: a customer at the till, or a screen that says "payment received". While records wait, they also hold memory in the accumulator, and once its 32 MiB is full, `send()` itself starts to wait. A longer deadline doesn't remove the unknown case either. It only moves it later, since a broker that's gone for an hour may never answer. So pick a deadline as long as your caller can wait, and handle the timeout as unknown.

try.title: Stall the broker past the deadline
steps: Open a second terminal in the `labs` folder and type this, without pressing Enter: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml pause kafka; sleep 8; docker compose -f env/kafka.yml unpause kafka`. `pause` freezes the broker's program in place without closing its connections, like the train in the tunnel.
In the first terminal, run the demo with a 5-second deadline (command below). It sends `pay-00` to `pay-29`, one every 500 ms. When `pay-10` appears, press Enter in the second terminal.

Read the failures and the last line. Then list the records written around the freeze, starting at the offset of the last fast record before the failures (2015 in the run below): `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic ledger-events --partition 0 --offset 2015 --max-messages 8 --formatter-property print.offset=true`.

package sfz.msg.l06.demo

import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.KafkaConsumer
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.KafkaProducer
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord
import org.apache.kafka.common.TopicPartition
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
import java.time.Duration

/**
 * Sends one payment every 500 ms for 15 seconds to "ledger-events" and prints how long each took to be
 * acknowledged, or why it failed. Pause the broker for a few seconds while it runs.
 * Arguments: "idempotent" (the default) or "plain" (idempotence off), then delivery.timeout.ms (default 10000).
 */
fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    val idempotent = args.firstOrNull() != "plain"
    val deadlineMs = args.getOrNull(1)?.toInt() ?: 10_000
    val tp = TopicPartition("ledger-events", 0)
    val consumerConfig = mapOf<String, Any>(
        "bootstrap.servers" to "localhost:9092",
        "key.deserializer" to StringDeserializer::class.java,
        "value.deserializer" to StringDeserializer::class.java,
    )
    val start = KafkaConsumer<String, String>(consumerConfig).use { it.endOffsets(listOf(tp)).getValue(tp) } // this run starts here

    val config = mapOf<String, Any>(
        "bootstrap.servers" to "localhost:9092",
        "key.serializer" to StringSerializer::class.java,
        "value.serializer" to StringSerializer::class.java,
        "enable.idempotence" to idempotent,
        "request.timeout.ms" to 2_000,      // give up on one request after 2 s, then retry
        "delivery.timeout.ms" to deadlineMs, // give up on the record this long after send()
    )
    println("idempotence ${if (idempotent) "on" else "off"}, delivery.timeout.ms $deadlineMs, request.timeout.ms 2000")
    KafkaProducer<String, String>(config).use { producer ->
        repeat(30) { i ->
            val id = "pay-%02d".format(i)
            val sentAt = System.nanoTime()
            producer.send(ProducerRecord("ledger-events", "acct-1", id)) { md, e ->
                val ms = (System.nanoTime() - sentAt) / 1_000_000
                if (e == null) println("%s acked after %5d ms at offset %d".format(id, ms, md.offset()))
                else println("%s FAILED after %4d ms: %s".format(id, ms, e::class.simpleName))
            }
            Thread.sleep(500)
        }
    }

    // what did the log get?
    val written = mutableListOf<String>()
    KafkaConsumer<String, String>(consumerConfig).use { c ->
        c.assign(listOf(tp))
        c.seek(tp, start)
        val end = c.endOffsets(listOf(tp)).getValue(tp)
        while (c.position(tp) < end) c.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500)).forEach { written += it.value() }
    }
    val distinct = written.toSet().size
    println("the log got ${written.size} records for $distinct different payments: ${written.size - distinct} duplicates")
}

sections.h: Retries can duplicate and reorder; the idempotent producer stops both
sections.body:
Retries cause two problems of their own. The first is duplicates. If the leader added a batch to the log and its answer was lost, the retry is added again. The leader has no way to tell a retry from a new record. A phone that resent the tunnel message on its own, without asking you, would do the same.

The second is reordering. With 5 requests in flight, request 1 can fail while requests 2 to 5 succeed. When request 1 is retried, its records land after the others. A refund can then overtake its payment inside one partition, which breaks the one order that Producers I: keys, partitions and ordering promised.

The simplest fix for reordering is one request in flight at a time. That works, but it limits each broker connection to one batch per round trip. Kafka's fix keeps 5 in flight and stops duplicates too: the **idempotent producer**. Idempotent means that doing something twice has the same effect as doing it once. It arrived in Kafka 0.11 and has been on by default since 3.0.

When it starts, the producer gets a producer id from the broker. It numbers the records it sends to each partition 0, 1, 2 and so on, and every batch carries the producer id and the **sequence number** of its first record. For each producer, the leader remembers the next sequence number it expects and the last 5 batches it added. Then:

- a batch with the next sequence number is added to the log;
- a retry of one of the last 5 batches is a duplicate: the leader writes nothing and answers with the offset it gave the first time;
- anything else is a gap. The leader refuses it with `OUT_OF_ORDER_SEQUENCE_NUMBER`, and the producer resends the missing batch first.

You may have met this idea already. Calling other services: REST, RPC and gRPC made a retried request safe with an idempotency key. The client sends the same key with every attempt, and the server remembers which keys it has handled. The idempotent producer is that idea built into Kafka's protocol, the rules for the messages between producer and broker. The key is the producer id plus the sequence number, and the leader is the server that remembers, for the last five batches.

That explains its three requirements: `acks=all`, `retries` above 0, and `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection` at most 5. Five is the number of batches the leader can recognise (`ProducerStateEntry.NUM_BATCHES_TO_RETAIN` in the broker's code). `acks=all` makes sure a batch the leader has confirmed, with its producer id and sequence number, is on every in-sync replica. So if the leader dies, the new leader rebuilds the same memory from its own copy of the log.

The requirements hide a trap. Set a conflicting value, such as `acks=1` for speed, without mentioning `enable.idempotence`, and the producer turns idempotence off without a word. There's no warning, and duplicates and reordering are back. If you set `enable.idempotence=true` yourself, the same conflict stops the producer at start-up with a `ConfigException`. So set it explicitly in every producer that sends payments. The lab checks both behaviours on a real broker.

**Retries are safe only when the broker can recognise them. Turn idempotence on by name.**

Know where the guarantee stops. It covers retries made by one producer, inside its delivery deadline. When your code catches a `TimeoutException` and calls `send()` again, that's a new record with a new sequence number, and it's written twice if the first one made it. That's you tapping Retry in the tunnel: to the app, your second tap was a new message. A restarted program also gets a new producer id. Duplicates across those lines need the app's own idempotency key, carried in the record and checked by the consumer.

```text
baseOffset: 2092 lastOffset: 2092 count: 1 baseSequence: 29 lastSequence: 29 producerId: 5 producerEpoch: 0 ...
```
Without idempotence, the frozen broker added `pay-16` to `pay-19` at offsets 2045 to 2048 when it woke, and then the retries added them again at 2049 to 2052, in reverse order. That's both problems from this section in one run: duplicates and reordering. With idempotence, the leader recognised the retries as duplicates, every payment was written once, and the offsets follow send order. The dump shows why: each batch carries the producer id and its sequence number, while the `plain` run's batches say `producerId: -1` and `baseSequence: -1`. Your counts depend on the timing of the freeze.

compare.note: Both pass a map of settings to the constructor; Java's `Map.of` takes up to ten pairs, which fits here. The callback's `e` is null when the send worked. Kotlin's `when (e)` with `is TimeoutException` reads as one table of cases, where Java needs a chain of `instanceof` checks. `TimeoutException` here is Kafka's own, `org.apache.kafka.common.errors.TimeoutException`, not the one in `java.util.concurrent`. The `outcome` is yours: something like a `CompletableFuture<Outcome>`, a value the calling code waits on, which ends up WRITTEN, FAILED or UNKNOWN.

recap: `send()` turns the record into bytes, picks the partition, adds the record to a batch in the accumulator and returns a Future. A separate sender thread sends ready batches, one request per broker.
A batch leaves when it's full (`batch.size`, 16 KB) or old enough (`linger.ms`, 5 ms since Kafka 4.0). Compression works per batch, so bigger batches compress better.

Retriable errors are retried automatically until `delivery.timeout.ms` (2 minutes) runs out. Then the send fails with a `TimeoutException`, which means unknown, not unwritten: the record may be in the log.

The idempotent producer (on by default since 3.0) is an idempotency key built into Kafka: a producer id plus sequence numbers. The leader drops retried duplicates and refuses gaps, so retries neither duplicate nor reorder.
Idempotence needs `acks=all`, `retries` above 0 and at most 5 requests in flight. A conflicting setting turns it off silently, unless you set `enable.idempotence=true` yourself.

The limit: it covers one producer's own retries. A second `send()` from your code, or a restarted program with a new producer id, can still write a payment twice, so the consumer needs the app's own idempotency key.
closing:
We started with a message sent twice from a train. A Kafka producer can do the same: a timeout means "I stopped waiting", and the payment may already be in the log. Its own retries are safe, thanks to producer ids and sequence numbers. A second `send()` from your code isn't.

If you write code that sends to Kafka, search it for `TimeoutException` and read what happens next. If the answer is "tell the customer it failed" or "send it again as a new payment", that's the train in the tunnel.

Next, we'll move to the other end of the log. We'll find out what a consumer must do so that a crash never loses a payment or applies it twice.

quiz.q: From The cluster: KRaft, replicas and the ISR. `payments` has replication factor 3 and `min.insync.replicas=2`. Two followers drop out of the ISR for 40 seconds, then return. A producer with default settings sends during that time. What happens to its sends?
options: They fail at once with NotEnoughReplicasException
They are written to the leader alone and acknowledged
The producer retries the NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS errors; the sends succeed once the ISR is back, well inside the 2-minute delivery.timeout.ms
They are dropped silently because the ISR is too small
quiz.why: `NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS` is retriable, so the producer keeps retrying, with pauses, and 40 seconds is well inside the 2-minute `delivery.timeout.ms`. Once the followers rejoin the ISR, the next attempt is accepted. Only an outage longer than the deadline would fail the send, and then with a `TimeoutException`, not `NotEnoughReplicasException`. The second option is what an `acks=1` producer would get.

quiz.q: To cut the wait for each answer, a team sets `acks=1` on its payment producer and changes nothing else. What else changed?
options: Idempotence is now off, silently, so retries can duplicate and reorder records
Nothing else: idempotence stays on by default
The producer fails at start-up with a ConfigException
Retries are disabled
quiz.why: Idempotence requires `acks=all`. When you haven't set `enable.idempotence` yourself, a conflicting setting turns it off without a warning; the lab's broker test shows the leader tracking no producer id afterwards. The ConfigException happens only when you also set `enable.idempotence=true` explicitly, which is why payment producers should.

quiz.q: A producer has `batch.size=16384` and `linger.ms=50`. A burst of 1,000 records of 100 bytes arrives within a millisecond, all for one partition. What does the sender do?
options: Waits 50 ms, then sends all 1,000 records in one batch
Sends 1,000 one-record requests
Waits 50 ms, then sends 7 batches
Sends 6 full batches of 163 records at once; the last 22 records wait up to 50 ms
quiz.why: A batch can't be bigger than `batch.size`, so 163 records of 100 bytes fill one, and a full batch may leave without waiting for `linger.ms`. Only the last, partly filled batch waits. The first option ignores `batch.size`, and `linger.ms` never holds back a full batch.

quiz.q: Your code catches a `TimeoutException` from `send()` and calls `send()` again with the same payment. Idempotence is on. The first attempt was in fact written. What does the log hold?
options: One copy: the idempotent producer recognises the resend
Two copies: the second `send()` is a new record with a new sequence number
One copy: the broker compares the values and drops the second
No copy: the broker removes the first record when the producer times out
quiz.why: Idempotence covers the producer's own retries of one batch, which reuse its sequence number. A second `send()` creates a new record with the next sequence number, so the leader adds it. The broker never compares values. That's why the consumer needs an idempotency key.

quiz.q: Your producer sends 50 records a second per partition with `linger.ms=5`. You raise it to 100 to get bigger batches. What happens?
options: Batches grow to about 5 records, and every record waits up to 100 ms longer
Batches fill to `batch.size` and latency drops
Nothing changes, because linger.ms only applies under heavy load
Throughput doubles and latency stays the same
quiz.why: At 50 records a second, 100 ms collects about 5 records, nowhere near 16 KB. The batches get a little bigger, and each record waits up to 100 ms longer. `linger.ms` matters most at moderate traffic; here it buys little and costs delay.

flashcards.front: What does `send()` do before it returns?
flashcards.back: It turns the key and value into bytes, picks the partition, adds the record to that partition's batch in the accumulator, and returns a Future. The sender thread does the network work.

flashcards.front: When does a batch leave the accumulator?
flashcards.back: When it's full (`batch.size`, 16,384 bytes by default) or when it has waited `linger.ms` (5 ms by default since Kafka 4.0), whichever comes first.
The whole time from `send()` returning to the final answer: batching, waiting, every retry. 2 minutes by default; then the send fails with a TimeoutException.

flashcards.front: A send fails with a TimeoutException. Is the record in the log?
flashcards.back: Maybe. The producer stopped waiting; the broker may have written it. Treat it as unknown, and send it again with the same idempotency key.

flashcards.front: How does the leader spot a retried batch from an idempotent producer?
flashcards.back: By the producer id and sequence numbers, Kafka's built-in idempotency key. It remembers the last 5 batches per producer and answers a repeat with the original offset, writing nothing.
A conflicting setting (`acks` other than all, `retries=0`, more than 5 requests in flight) when `enable.idempotence` wasn't set explicitly.

flashcards.front: What doesn't the idempotent producer protect against?
flashcards.back: Your code calling `send()` twice, a restarted producer (new producer id), or anything beyond one partition. Those need idempotency keys or transactions.

terms.plain: The producer's buffer of batches, one queue per partition. `send()` adds to it; the sender thread takes from it.
Records for one partition that travel and are stored together, and are compressed as one unit.
How long a batch may wait for more records before it leaves. 5 ms by default since Kafka 4.0.
The most bytes a batch may hold. A full batch leaves without waiting for `linger.ms`.
A broker error that may pass on its own, such as NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER. The producer retries it automatically.
The deadline for a record, from `send()` to the final answer, covering all retries. 2 minutes by default.
A producer whose retries can't duplicate or reorder records in a partition, thanks to a producer id and sequence numbers. On by default since Kafka 3.0.
The number an idempotent producer gives each record it sends to a partition: 0, 1, 2 and so on. Each batch carries the number of its first record.

explain_back.prompt: Someone new on your team asks: "We have idempotence on, so we can never get duplicate payments in Kafka, right?" Explain what idempotence does, how, and where it stops.
explain_back.answer: It stops one kind of duplicate. When the producer retries a batch because the answer got lost, the leader would normally add it again. With idempotence, the producer has a producer id and numbers every record per partition. So on the retry, the leader sees the same producer id and sequence number, finds it among the last five batches it remembers, writes nothing and returns the original offset. Gaps are refused too, so retries can't reorder records either. But it only covers that producer's own retries. If our code gets a TimeoutException and calls send again, that's a new record with a new sequence number, and if the first one made it, we have two. A restarted program also gets a new producer id. So we still put an idempotency key on every payment, and the consumer skips keys it has already applied. And someone setting acks=1 without enable.idempotence=true would turn it off silently, so we set it explicitly.

deeper.body:
Look at the dump from the Try it with the 5-second deadline, if you kept the broker. The batches after the failures say `producerEpoch: 1`, and their sequence numbers start again at 0. When a batch runs out of time, the producer can't know whether the leader added it, so its sequence numbers might now have a gap the leader would refuse forever. Since Kafka 2.5 (KIP-360; a KIP is a Kafka Improvement Proposal), the idempotent producer handles this by raising its **epoch**, a counter kept next to the producer id, and starting its sequence numbers again at 0. The leader accepts sequence 0 from a newer epoch. Transactions and exactly-once uses the same epoch to shut out an old copy of a producer that wakes up after it was replaced. Since Kafka 4.0 (KIP-890), producers that use transactions raise it on every transaction.

Two more settings change the picture. `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=1` keeps order without idempotence, at the cost of one round trip per batch to each broker; with idempotence, there's no reason to lower it. The producer documentation advises keeping `request.timeout.ms` (30 seconds by default) larger than the brokers' `replica.lag.time.max.ms` (also 30 seconds). With `acks=all`, a slow follower can hold an answer back for up to that long, and timing out earlier only adds retries and, without idempotence, duplicates. The Try its used 2 seconds only to make the freeze show up quickly.

Finally, `acks=0`. The producer sends and forgets: no answer, no offset (the answer says -1), no retries that could help, and idempotence is off. It suits measurements or debugging messages you can afford to lose, never payments.
